title: H4/K1: copying a sea watch and keeping it navigationally useful
summary: A commissioned copy separated Harrison's demonstration from another maker's execution; later cleaning, corrosion and astronomical checks separated precision manufacture from durable navigational service.

stages.invention: H4 is treated as the antecedent device; no sole-inventor or first-chronometer claim.
stages.feasibility: Kendall's K1 completed in 1769 and tested on Cook's second voyage; one replication, not a production yield.
stages.deployment: Named Cook voyage trials and service, followed by cleaning and further use.
stages.diffusion: Not estimated; these state-supported voyages cannot stand for merchant or naval fleets.
stages.scaling: K1 replication does not establish cheap or rapid repeated production.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Contemporary alternatives included astronomical methods and dead reckoning; simplified watch accounts do not identify a uniform performance gain.
stages.displacement/reversal: K1 reportedly stopped and needed replacement parts; astronomical practice remained complementary.

counterevidence: The contemporary obituary praises Kendall and disputes cannot be resolved without original trial data. Other chronometer designs and other navigation methods limit any H4-centred genealogy.

episode.technology_configuration: Harrison H4 copied by Kendall as K1, operated with rate knowledge and astronomical observations aboard specified voyages.
episode.task: Infer longitude from reference time compared with local time while preserving a usable timekeeper during long voyages.
episode.population: Kendall, Board of Longitude evaluators and Cook expedition officers; broader shipping populations not measured.
episode.interval: 1766 commission; 1769 completion; second and third Cook voyages in the 1770s; contextual practices to c.1800.
contemporary_alternatives: Lunar-distance observations with instruments and tables
episode.adoption_measure: One named surviving copy and documented trial/service episodes; no fleet denominator or diffusion rate.
episode.observation_limits: Completion and approximate delivery dates differ between S01 and S02. Reports do not provide comparable staffing, costs, breakdown exposure or voyage outcomes.

actors.chooser: Board commissioners commissioned and allocated trials; naval expedition leadership used the instrument.
actors.payer: Board/state supplied commissioned instruments and trial resources; no audited all-in cost is claimed.
actors.operator_maintainer: Skilled maker and service personnel; expedition astronomers/officers observed and compared times. Supporting crew labour is not quantified.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Crews and communities encountered by expeditions; this instrument evidence does not isolate consequences for them.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Commission was a negotiated maker contract. The sources do not establish individual crew consent or ability to choose a different navigation system.

labour.tasks: Precision copying, adjustment, cleaning, part replacement, rating and observation; commissioned craft was paid, shipboard task allocation and unpaid support unquantified.
labour.entry_barriers: Established watchmaking ability, access to mechanism/explanation and state evaluation; no estimate of apprenticeship returns.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Commissioners controlled test acceptance and resource allocation; Kendall's copying obligation did not equal a guarantee of performance in the obituary's account.
labour.transition: Several years from commission to completed copy, followed by multi-year voyages; no occupational cohort evidence.
labour.distribution: Recognised makers and officers are visible; wages, workshops' gains and ordinary mariners' welfare are not established.
labour.evidence_limit: Demonstrates distinct tasks supporting practical precision, not net job creation, equal access or the invention's social return.

title: Japanese seasonal clocks and Tanaka's unscaled automatic clock
region: Japan: Kyoto, Kurume, Saga and surviving museum collections
summary: Japanese makers used adjustable rates or hour markers to serve seasonal hours. Tanaka's automatic variant was an exceptional artifact, not evidence that its complexity translated into sales or a replicable production system.

stages.invention: European mechanical designs were antecedents; local seasonal-hour mechanisms included several distinct configurations.
stages.feasibility: Surviving mechanisms and disassembly establish how adjustments were implemented; original rate stability is not remeasured here.
stages.deployment: Seasonal clocks were used; Tanaka made one Myriad Year Clock in 1851.
stages.diffusion: Surviving collection is not a population ownership curve; prototype's distribution stayed singular in S04's account.
stages.scaling: Tanaka intended additional sales, but S04 reports one unsold clock; no unit cost series.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Manually adjusted seasonal clocks remained the practical comparison to the elaborate automated variant.
stages.displacement/reversal: Seiko describes gradual disappearance following fixed-hour reform in 1873, not immediate universal replacement.

counterevidence: The unsold-clock story is a biographical account with an anecdotal cost explanation; many records were destroyed. A masterpiece is selected precisely because it is unusual.

episode.technology_configuration: Seasonal clocks with alternately operating foliots or manually shifted hour markers; Tanaka's 1851 automatic hour-marker arrangement is an explicitly distinguished subconfiguration.
episode.task: Display locally meaningful hours that change with seasonal day/night duration, and in Tanaka's artifact combine several calendars/displays.
episode.population: Documented makers, users of surviving clock types and prospective elite buyers of Tanaka's clock; not all Japanese households.
episode.interval: Early/mid-nineteenth-century configurations, Tanaka's 1847 instruction and 1851 clock, contextual 1873 reform.
contemporary_alternatives: Equal-hour imported clocks with conversion to local practice
Public time signals and nonmechanical timekeeping; comparative cost not established
episode.adoption_measure: Surviving mechanism types and single prototype history; qualitative post-reform decline. No sales/household denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Elite survival bias, uncertain tool reconstruction and anecdotal purchaser refusal. Later disassembly diagnoses construction, not historical user satisfaction.

actors.chooser: Makers designed for existing time conventions; owners/users chose clock variants; government later changed the legal time system.
actors.payer: Customers and patrons in Tanaka's career; intended elite purchaser for the masterpiece was not secured in the source's account.
actors.operator_maintainer: Users or clockmakers periodically repositioned markers/adjusted foliots; identities and remuneration of routine winders are not established.
actors.affected_nonchooser: People following shared time signals and workers serving clock owners; specific effects not measured.
actors.ability_to_refuse: The reported buyer could decline the clock. A national time-system change is not proof of every user's voluntary preference; enforcement and compliance are unmeasured.

labour.tasks: Design, fine metalworking, clock adjustment and calendrical interpretation; automatic markers could remove a recurring adjustment task for this configuration, but no labour saving was measured.
labour.entry_barriers: Craft ability, access to specialist calendar teaching, tools and patronage; actual tools for Tanaka's fine gears are incompletely known.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Tanaka ran a commercial shop and later served a feudal patron; no general guild ownership or wage structure inferred.
labour.transition: Named career sequence across the 1840s–1850s, not a cohort of clockmakers after 1873.
labour.distribution: An unusually successful maker is visible; ordinary makers, household staff and women are poorly represented.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot establish widespread deskilling, unemployment after reform, average affordability or that tacit skills were uniquely necessary.

title: Harpers Ferry: precision machinery, verified gauges and incomplete uniformity
region: United States: Harpers Ferry and comparison with Springfield
summary: Hall's state-funded rifle works, the main musket factory and later inspection equipment show why a patent, a machine and an interchangeable output population are separate observations.

stages.invention: Hall's rifle patent dated 1811 preceded the 1819 production contract; milling-machine origin is not assigned to one person.
stages.feasibility: Contemporary Hall/Talcott testimony describes uniform rifle manufacture; it is not a tolerance audit of all output.
stages.deployment: Precision machines and gauges introduced across distinct works, at different dates.
stages.diffusion: Qualitative inter-armory transmission and later gauge artifacts; no all-industry adoption rate.
stages.scaling: Contracted batch manufacture and annual musket output existed, but this contribution does not infer universal interchangeability from volumes.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Older Model 1816 muskets retained incomplete interchangeability in 1829 tests; established craft production coexisted with change.
stages.displacement/reversal: Machinery and divided work reduced some hand operations; complete disappearance of skilled labour is not demonstrated.

counterevidence: Different gun models and workshops are not matched treatments. Machinery could reduce handwork without lowering total costs or improving worker welfare; institutional narratives overemphasise celebrated innovators.

episode.technology_configuration: Hall's breechloading-rifle works (from 1819), distinct main musket-factory standardisation, and Model 1841 inspection-gauge set ca.1846.
episode.task: Produce and inspect repeatable components, reducing reliance on individually fitted finished firearms.
episode.population: Specified armory workshops, inspectors and batches/models; not all US manufacturing or all arms at Harpers Ferry.
episode.interval: 1816 machinery/Model 1816 changes; 1819 Hall contract; 1823 gauges; 1829 tests of earlier muskets; ca.1846 surviving inspection set.
contemporary_alternatives: Hand fitting components to individual arms
episode.adoption_measure: Dated machinery/gauge use, named correspondence and retrospective account of specific tests. No component-level pass-rate denominator recovered.
episode.observation_limits: Original inspection report and payrolls not independently inspected. NPS sources share Smith/Schmidt lineage; HAFE7427 is a later set, not Hall's original tooling.

actors.chooser: War Department/Ordnance authorities, Hall and armory superintendents made overlapping procurement and production decisions.
actors.payer: Federal government contracts, workshops and inspection resources.
actors.operator_maintainer: Paid mechanics and operatives; skilled makers of machine tools/gauges and inspectors; exact staffing and skill composition unavailable.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers subject to changed piece rates/task organisation; soldiers and people subjected to military force, whose outcomes are not measured here.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Superintendent resistance is documented, but individual workers' bargaining or exit options require evidence beyond management testimony.

labour.tasks: Some hand fitting moved to machine setup, repeated operations and gauging; main factory had piecework and 55 occupations by 1816, predating Hall's arrival.
labour.entry_barriers: Making/calibrating tools differed from operating them; Hall asserted that ordinary workmen could produce uniform arms, but entry training time is unmeasured.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Government controlled procurement and inspectors; Hall held a design patent. Machinery's distributional gains and patent-contract income are not quantified.
labour.transition: Several decades with uneven workshops and models; not an instantaneous system switch or individual-worker panel.
labour.distribution: Managerial claims of economy are not evidence of higher wages, lower injuries or net employment gains.
labour.evidence_limit: Identifies reorganised tasks and quality control; cannot identify net deskilling or unit-cost advantage after toolmaking and inspection costs.

title: Tanzanian automotive workshops: learning, tool ownership and repair alternatives
region: Tanzania: Dar es Salaam, Morogoro, Tabora and other documented garages
summary: Workshop learning and salvage could keep vehicles operating without purchasing new ones, while labour obligations, tool accumulation and disagreements over reliability shaped who could become an independent mechanic.

stages.invention: Specific repairs recombined existing parts and processes; no claim of a national original automobile invention.
stages.feasibility: Observed repairs and interview histories identify working practices; no standardised lifetime or road-safety experiment.
stages.deployment: Named garages and repairs documented through interviews, photographs and author participation.
stages.diffusion: Pedagogic lineages and regional differences described qualitatively; no workshop census or national rate.
stages.scaling: Tool accumulation and more customers sometimes enabled a larger workshop, but one career does not establish typical upward mobility.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Mechanics sometimes preferred keeping modules original and specialising by model rather than maximising modification.
stages.displacement/reversal: Repair extended older vehicles' use; no aggregate displacement of new vehicle sales or formal training is inferred.

counterevidence: Coastal mechanics contested some upcountry methods; makers themselves associated some improvisation with bad economic conditions. Successful survivors and male technical authority dominate the record.

episode.technology_configuration: Informal gereji bubu performing routine maintenance, part modification and modular reuse on heterogeneous motor vehicles.
episode.task: Return existing vehicles to service and train mechanics under changing parts availability and cash constraints.
episode.population: Grace's named mechanics and workshops; historical recollections of 1960s–1980s careers plus directly observed training/repairs in 2011–2012.
episode.interval: Historical skill/parts trajectories and later field observation are separately identified; direct observation is not projected unchanged into the past.
contemporary_alternatives: Keep stock modules versus extensive modification
episode.adoption_measure: Specific repair histories, table 2.1's interview-linked methods, workshop observations and one narrated shop expansion; no representative rates.
episode.observation_limits: Retrospective recall, one researcher's short apprenticeship, selected reputationally visible mechanics and no independently measured repair durability.

actors.chooser: Vehicle owners choose repairs subject to cost/parts; head mechanics choose methods and allocate apprentice access.
actors.payer: Customers pay for jobs; apprentices contribute labour while receiving instruction and reported small shares of profits rather than a regular salary; occasional earnings from assisting repairs are also described.
actors.operator_maintainer: Head mechanics, specialists and apprentices; apprentices also cooked, cleaned and did household errands.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Passengers, other road users and youths allocated risky or menial work; outcomes not systematically recorded.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Independent work became possible with skills/tools; cash and job scarcity constrained entry choices. No universal freedom or coercion finding for apprentices is warranted.

labour.tasks: Routine servicing, heavy lifting, grinding, diagnosis, fabrication, tool salvage, domestic support and teaching. Labour-for-learning exchange is visible, not a paid/unpaid binary.
labour.entry_barriers: Access to a supervising mechanic, years of participation, personal tools, bodily work and reputation; some accounts cite unaffordable formal schooling.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Apprentices' personal tool stocks increased independent-job options; senior mechanics controlled customer relationships and specialist-learning opportunities.
labour.transition: Named life histories and observed hierarchy suggest long progression; no typical completion rate, earnings trajectory or cohort denominator.
labour.distribution: Workshops offered entry but exposed youths to physical risk and menial work; gendered masculine authority is documented, women's full role not measured.
labour.evidence_limit: Practical access is not proof of secure income, safe repair, universal opportunity or positive aggregate welfare.

title: Dar es Salaam electrical repair: sustaining appliance access under unreliable supply
summary: Repair technicians supplied an intermediate service between an appliance purchase and ongoing usable electricity. Consumer accounts support particular restorations, while population effects and the technical durability of modifications remain untested.

stages.invention: Not a new appliance principle; existing devices and components were repaired or modified.
stages.feasibility: Customers reported working repaired appliances; engineering validation of modified protection is absent.
stages.deployment: Appliance services and repair kiosks documented in fieldwork, newspaper accounts and interviews.
stages.diffusion: Qualitative growth in device and repair use; no appliance-owning household denominator.
stages.scaling: Not quantified; recurring breakdown can expand repair demand without improving underlying grid performance.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Backup generation was financially bounded, and households could keep repaired/second-hand devices rather than replace them.
stages.displacement/reversal: Source proposes formal utility retrenchment feeding informal work; causal allocation and worker outcomes remain underdetermined.

counterevidence: Author emphasises resilience; successful repair testimony may omit failed repairs. Appliance import growth and market liberalisation may drive service demand as much as power failure. Utility workforce claims do not isolate computerisation from policy cuts.

episode.technology_configuration: Household appliance diagnosis, power-supply/component repair and technician advice; utility-side work appears only as an explicitly separate labour-supply context.
episode.task: Restore or preserve household appliance use despite damage and volatile electricity service.
episode.population: Interviewed electricity users and technicians in Dar es Salaam; no representative city sample is claimed.
episode.interval: Historical frame 1985–2020; direct interviews in 2018/2020; older labour histories reconstructed using other evidence.
contemporary_alternatives: Retain an older repaired or second-hand device
episode.adoption_measure: Qualitative interview reports, including continued use after repair, and observed kiosks; no denominator, market share or aggregate failure rate.
episode.observation_limits: Anonymous interviews protect sensitive participants but restrict rechecking; author-translated accounts and retrospective claims are not independent electrical tests.

actors.chooser: Householders choose repair/backup expenditures; technicians propose parts and interventions.
actors.payer: Householders bear repair and interruption costs; payment schedules and informal credit are not systematically described.
actors.operator_maintainer: Formally and informally trained technicians; household operation and care are not time-budgeted.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Other household members and neighbours share service/safety consequences; unequal backup access is described without a group-level welfare measure.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Repair versus replacement is constrained by cash and service availability. Utility-side vishoka work has a distinct legal status and is not equated with ordinary appliance repair.

labour.tasks: Diagnosis, component replacement, wiring/advice and practical learning after formal schooling; adjacent temporary utility work can supply experience.
labour.entry_barriers: Schooling, workshop practice, tools, customers and contacts; formal qualifications alone do not record practical experience.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Freelancers obtain fee income but lack the employment position of utility staff; exact earnings/security not measured.
labour.transition: Mchome links 1990s utility retrenchment to street electrical work, but no individual/cohort panel allocates effects between technology and structural adjustment.
labour.distribution: Some households report access restored at lower cost than replacement; no citywide affordability claim or safety gain is established.
labour.evidence_limit: Repair demand is not a welfare measure; cannot establish that displaced utility workers regained former pay, security or bargaining power.

title: Early TEA-laser replication: contact, specifications and material failure
summary: A contemporary network study reports failed written-only builds and successful contact-linked builds, but also failed visits, unnecessarily strict specifications and component breakdowns. It supports bounded transfer mechanisms rather than an untestable necessity of tacit knowledge.

stages.invention: Origin laboratory built early devices before public announcement; publication date is not the invention date.
stages.feasibility: Operating beams supplied an observable success criterion for configurations in the study; reliability varied.
stages.deployment: Seven identified British labs were building/using devices in summer 1971, with North American source-lab contacts investigated subsequently.
stages.diffusion: Purposive problem-defined network with explicit searches for isolates; no total world-lab denominator.
stages.scaling: Commercial variants and a British purchase after failed construction were reported; no manufacturing yield or sales series.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Some attempts failed or were abandoned; alternative fabrication and buying a finished device supplied different routes.
stages.displacement/reversal: No general displacement of publications or theory; detailed instructions improved and hardware failures persisted.

counterevidence: Contact was not randomised, some contacts failed, and inexperienced or poorly resourced labs may differ systematically. Collins explicitly allowed written-only success and acknowledged purposive selection of a favourable example.

episode.technology_configuration: Early transversely excited atmospheric-pressure CO2 lasers, with pin-bar and double-discharge models distinguished where construction details differ.
episode.task: Obtain an operating laser beam, either to develop the instrument or use it in other experiments.
episode.population: Seven identified British labs and investigated North American source labs; a 1975 follow-up builder is a separately identified episode.
episode.interval: 1968 antecedent operation; 1970 announcement; 1971 interviews and later follow-ups through 1975.
contemporary_alternatives: Visits, telephone assistance or personnel movement
Purchase a commercial laser once available
episode.adoption_measure: Named but pseudonymised labs' operating/nonoperating devices, interview network and one reported British commercial purchase; no general adoption percentage.
episode.observation_limits: Snowball selection checked by questionnaires, funding records and citations; unsuccessful isolates still may be missed. No randomised exposure, complete cost comparison or uniform performance threshold.

actors.chooser: Laboratory scientists/managers chose build routes and disclosures; instrument need differed between laser-development and downstream experiments.
actors.payer: Government/university research resources and commercial licence customers; comparative full build/purchase costs not audited.
actors.operator_maintainer: Researchers, technical staff, machinists and commercial consultants; their paid/unpaid hours are not separated.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Students and staff allocated to build/support work; subsequent application impacts are outside this case.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Labs could withhold details or buy/abandon, but grant/resource constraints mattered. Individual junior researchers' refusal options are unknown.

labour.tasks: Machining, assembly, debugging, consulting, visiting and instruction; improved specification can redirect work to suppliers as well as people learning in-house.
labour.entry_barriers: Prior laboratory expertise, equipment and access to experienced builders; contacts could be governed by reciprocity and competition.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Variants were patented/licensed while articles and assistance circulated; researchers also guarded unpatented practical information for reputational competition.
labour.transition: Build attempts over weeks/months and transfers/placements are described, not occupational displacement or lifetime earnings.
labour.distribution: Experienced gatekeepers held attention and information advantages; effects on junior staff, technicians or public benefit are not quantified.
labour.evidence_limit: Shows specific communication/material bottlenecks, not that more funding never helps or that all instrument knowledge is unwriteable.
